text: Immutable time-partitioned blocks over the retained log, optional min/max and Bloom block summaries, selective columnar Parquet projection, postings or materialized views for hot terms, adaptive indexes, OTel sidecar collection, and later offload to object storage or hardware; accelerators are disposable caches rebuilt from raw evidence, and missing summaries fall back to full scans.
Completeness is a property of the reader's scan: a query is complete because it evaluated every candidate row, and the set of blocks it iterates over is implicitly trusted to be the whole snapshot.
origin: Zone maps and small materialized aggregates came from single-node warehouses where the engine owned the heap file, so the block list could not be silently short; the S1 probe inherits this by owning all rows in RAM.

text: The durable commit of one record requires ordering by two syncs: sync the frame, then write and sync a commit marker.
origin: WAL practice on disks without ordering primitives: ordering was only obtainable by waiting for a flush; ADR-0005/0006 chose it for a per-event lesson, and Stage 6 found 99.965-99.969% of pipeline time inside append.

text: Indexing is a separate phase after ingest: summaries are derived later from committed rows and published independently, so they can be missing or stale relative to the rows.
origin: Batch ETL and Lucene refresh separated write durability from search visibility because index build was expensive relative to the write; in Fabric the writer already touches every byte and waits on sync.

text: Row identity and duplicate preservation come from physical position in one single-writer log; checking that every acknowledged event reached the durable owner requires comparing full event sequences.
origin: FOL2 single-writer design and the CLI's prefix check against a deterministic generator; EventId is not globally unique, so position is the only identity available.

text: A query result is a list of rows; coverage (which blocks were examined, which were unavailable) is implicit, so a query either succeeds completely or fails.
origin: SQL closed-world semantics on a local database, where partial availability was a crash, not a normal state.

text: Absence of a value in a block is proven either by exhaustive row inspection or by a probabilistic positive summary (Bloom); raw evidence is stored in its ingest byte representation.
origin: Bloom filters answer membership with one-sided error and were cheap to bolt on; storing raw bytes verbatim made reconstruction trivial.

text: S1 proves no false negatives for summaries, yet the proof assumes the iterated block set is the complete snapshot; nothing attests that the block list itself is complete, so a missing block and a legitimately empty region are indistinguishable to the summary layer.

Stage 6 puts 99.965-99.969% of pipeline time inside the two-sync append (340-395 events/s), while the research effort targets query pruning that saves tens to hundreds of microseconds in RAM; the expensive boundary and the optimized boundary are different.

The log's torn-tail rule is deterministic only because of sync ordering, yet corruption detection already rests on CRC32, which the docs say is not authentication; the system mixes an ordering-based guarantee with a checksum-based one and treats only the first as exact.

After a failed sync the file alone cannot reveal that earlier acknowledged records were lost, so the no-ACK-before-durable-owner contract has no runtime detector: violations are only preventable, never observable.

title: Indexes that never record their own omissions
noticed: Every accelerator in the baseline describes what is present in a block; none describes which blocks exist, so the S1 proof silently needs an unlisted premise (T1).
why_possible: A commit record can carry arbitrary committed metadata, including a digest of prior commits; hash chaining and Merkle trees are well-established, so binding coverage to commit violates no known law.
standpoint: A historian in 2126 explaining why 2020s observability stores could not tell an empty answer from a lost shard

title: The sync shadow is free compute
noticed: Stage 6: 99.965-99.969% of pipeline wall time is inside append, mostly waiting on two syncs; S1 builds a 64-row block summary in 39-2,207 microseconds, smaller than typical sync latency.
why_possible: CPU work overlapped with a blocking device flush consumes no extra wall time if it fits in the wait; no law ties summary construction to a later phase.
standpoint: The phenomenon itself: the writer already reads every byte and then idles

title: Double-entry bookkeeping for ACKs
noticed: The sender retains until ACK and the receiver commits before ACK: two ledgers describing the same set, but nobody ever reconciles them, so lost-after-ACK (T4) is invisible.
why_possible: Set reconciliation with invertible Bloom lookup tables recovers the exact symmetric difference in space proportional to the difference, and reports decode failure explicitly; nothing forbids running it between sender retention and durable owner.
standpoint: An accountant who reconciles two ledgers by their difference, not by re-reading every entry

title: Coverage receipts: the commit chain attests the block set, the query returns proof of what it did not read
idea: Invert who owns completeness: the writer, not the reader. Each block seal extends a hash chain seal_k = H(seal_{k-1} || block_id || row_count || H(block bytes) || H(summary bytes)). A query returns rows plus a receipt: the chain head it ran against and, for every block, either scanned or rejected-by-summary-digest-d or unavailable. A verifier replays the receipt against the chain: a dropped block, a reordered block, or a summary from another snapshot (the agenda's stale-Bloom counterexample) breaks the chain or the digest and is detected; an empty answer is only complete when the receipt covers every sealed block. Missing acceleration becomes scanned; missing data becomes an explicit unavailable entry, never an empty result.
kill_test: Pre-register 3 injected defects (deleted block, stale summary, swapped block order) x 12 S1 snapshots plus 12 clean controls. Kill if any defect receipt verifies, any clean receipt fails, or verifying a receipt reads any row bytes; also kill if sealing adds an extra sync per block versus the unsealed writer (count syncs with strace).
thought_experiment: Idealised: a snapshot of 32 blocks where block 17 holds the only match for a rare token. Case a, block 17 file deleted: the reader's block list has 31 entries; the receipt cannot reproduce seal_32 and the verifier rejects the empty answer. Case b, block 17 present but its Bloom replaced by the previous snapshot's Bloom (which lacks the token): the query skips it, but the receipt names digest d_old, which is not the digest in seal_17, so the rejection is refused. Case c, correct: the receipt reproduces seal_32. The prediction is that all three cases are decided by hashing only seals and summaries, never by rereading rows.

title: Remove the ordering sync: content-bound group seals decide torn tails
idea: Subtract the first sync. Write a group of frames and one seal record, then issue a single sync; the seal holds the group's byte length and a collision-resistant hash (e.g. SHA-256) over all frame bytes. Recovery accepts a group iff its seal is present and the hash over the preceding bytes matches; otherwise the whole unsealed group is truncated. Ordering is replaced by content binding: whichever subset of the group's writes reached media before a crash, a partial group cannot match its seal. ACK is still sent only after the single sync returns, so the durable-owner contract is unchanged; the reliance on hash collision resistance is an explicit, stated assumption that replaces the current reliance on CRC32 plus write ordering.
kill_test: Enumerate every subset of persisted sectors for groups of 1..6 frames with a write-permutation crash simulator (dm-log-writes style replay over a loop device, or a pure-Rust sector model); kill if any recovery exposes a non-prefix, a partially persisted group, or loses a group whose sync returned. Separately kill the performance motive if durable events/s at group size 1 is not at least 1.5x the two-sync baseline on the Stage 6 host.
thought_experiment: Idealised device that persists any subset of the written 4 KiB sectors in any order before a crash. Two-sync design: safe by ordering. One-sync seal design: every subset either contains all group sectors (seal verifies) or omits one (seal hash mismatches or the seal is absent), so recovery yields exactly the prefix of fully persisted groups. Prediction: for all 2^n subsets of an n-sector group, the recovered set equals a group-aligned prefix, and no ACKed group is ever lost after the sync returns.

title: Residual answers: a query returns exact rows plus an exact residual query over what it could not read
idea: Change the unit of a query answer from rows to a pair (rows R_c, residual q_r) where R_c is exactly R restricted to covered sealed blocks and q_r is the same predicate restricted to the named uncovered blocks. Answers compose: running q_r later and merging by block position yields exactly R, preserving arrival order and duplicates. Unavailable, cold or corrupt blocks do not turn into errors or silent empties; they become residual work with an identity. Completeness is then a monotone property the client can drive to closure, and cost can be spent lazily on the residual only when the client needs closure.
kill_test: Over the S1 corpus, draw 1,000 random availability masks per snapshot and random re-availability orders; kill if any composed answer differs from the full-scan position list, any answer with empty residual omits a sealed block, or merge-by-position fails on duplicate EventIds.
thought_experiment: Snapshot with 4 blocks, block 2 offline. Classical: fail the query or silently return blocks 0,1,3. Residual: return rows of 0,1,3 in position order plus residual {q, block 2}. When block 2 returns, the residual yields its rows, merged by position into exactly the full-scan list. Prediction: for any availability schedule, the fold of partial answers equals the full-scan reference, and an answer with an empty residual is never produced while a sealed block is unread.

title: Reconcile the ACK ledgers: IBLT difference between sender retention and durable owner
idea: Transplant set reconciliation from networking into the delivery contract. The sender keeps an invertible Bloom lookup table over the (producer, sequence, record-hash) tuples it has seen ACKed in an epoch; the durable owner keeps one over the tuples it has sealed. Subtracting the two tables and peeling decodes the exact symmetric difference when it is small, in space and time proportional to the difference, not the epoch. Outcome is three-valued: empty difference, an exact listed difference (ACKed but not durable = contract violation with names, durable but never ACKed = safe duplicate candidate), or decode failure, which triggers a full sequence comparison, never an assumed match. This gives T4 a runtime detector, including after the fsync failure the log cannot see, without per-event cross-checking. Duplicates are keyed by position via the sequence, not EventId.
kill_test: Simulate epochs of 10^4..10^6 tuples with injected loss d in {0,1,3,30,300} and duplicate retries; kill if any run with d>0 reports an empty difference, any decode lists a wrong tuple, or audit bytes exchanged exceed 1% of a full tuple exchange at d<=30. Report the empirically observed false-empty rate (expected 0) and the checksum width it relies on.
thought_experiment: Epoch of 10^6 ACKed events; a storage writeback failure silently drops 3 already-ACKed records. Full audit reads 10^6 tuples on both sides. IBLT with ~60 cells subtracts to a table whose peel lists exactly those 3 tuples on the sender side. If 10^4 records were lost, peeling fails, which is reported as undecodable and forces the full compare. Prediction: detection cost scales with the loss, not the epoch, and the audit never reports no-loss when loss occurred except under a hash collision stated as an assumption.

title: The commit marker is the block summary: acceleration that cannot be stale
idea: Unify durability and indexing into one object. The commit record for a block carries its time min/max, exact tenant set and token summary, and the durable commit is that record's sync; summaries are computed in the sync shadow of the block's frames. Consequences: a committed block without a summary cannot exist, a summary without its rows cannot be committed, and staleness is impossible by construction because the summary is the commit. Rebuild from raw evidence remains possible and is a verification step (recompute and compare), not a recovery necessity. Missing-acceleration fallback survives only for pre-upgrade blocks.
kill_test: Crash-inject at every write boundary of 1,000 sealed blocks and verify that every recovered committed block's embedded summary equals a fresh recomputation; kill on any mismatch. Kill the cost claim if median durable block commit latency rises more than 3% versus the same writer without embedded summaries, over 20 paired trials on the Stage 6 host.
thought_experiment: Idealised device with 2 ms sync and a CPU that builds a 64-row summary in 0.9 ms. Separate-phase design: ingest wall time T plus an index build phase and a publication step that can crash between rows and summary. Unified design: wall time T (summary overlaps sync), zero publication window. Prediction: no crash point exists where rows are durable and the summary is absent or belongs to other rows; wall time per durable block is unchanged within noise.

title: Exact absence by lossless decomposition, gated at the ACK boundary
idea: Treat the tolerated near-coincidence that most log bytes are templates plus variables as exact: store each event as (template id, typed variables) and per block the exact dictionaries of templates and variable values present. A token absent from both dictionaries is exactly absent from the block, a deterministic certificate with no Bloom collisions. The contract twist: before ACK, the writer decodes the stored form and compares bytes with the original using the same exact comparison as same_record_contents; an event that does not round-trip bit-identically is stored verbatim instead. Lossless reconstruction is then a durability-boundary invariant, not a compression property.
kill_test: On a pinned public log corpus (Loghub subset, hash recorded) and the S1 corpus: kill if any event fails bit-identical round trip without falling back to verbatim, if any dictionary-excluded block contains the token, or if dictionary bytes per block exceed the raw block bytes for more than half of blocks.
thought_experiment: Block of 64 logs sharing 3 templates. Query token 'timeout': it appears in neither the template dictionary nor the variable dictionary, so the block is exactly excluded; a Bloom of the same byte budget could admit it on collision but never exclude falsely. Prediction: exact exclusion equals Bloom exclusion plus the false-positive blocks, with zero false negatives, and every stored event reconstructs to identical bytes including -0.0 and NaN payload bits.

title: I1r Authenticated coverage with a validated summary builder (repairs I1)
idea: Completeness is attested by the writer, under stated trust. A trusted, validated summary builder refuses to seal a block unless every row's exact S1 tokens, tenant and time fall inside the summary (checked against rows at seal time, not assumed). Each block commitment c_i = H(i, row_digest, summary_digest, builder_and_tokenizer_version); a snapshot root is a Merkle root over c_0..c_{n-1} together with n and a snapshot id, and the root and count come from an independently trusted channel. A query receipt lists a disposition for every ordinal 0..n-1 with its Merkle path: scanned (names row_digest), rejected (includes summary bytes, and the verifier re-runs the exclusion rule on them for the query), or unavailable. The verifier checks paths, count, digests and the exclusion rule without reading row bytes. A scanned disposition does not prove the scan executed: the executor is assumed non-malicious, and row-level exactness is checked against an independent full-scan oracle in tests. SHA-256 collision resistance is assumed; CRC32 is not an equivalent assumption.
kill_test: See prereg E1: 7 defect classes x 12 fresh-seed snapshots x 128 queries plus clean controls; violations = undetected defects + false rejections + result != full-scan oracle + receipt verification reading row bytes; kill if violations > 0. Non-vacuity: original I1 chain-only verifier must miss the sealed-false-negative and replaced-head defects.
thought_experiment: Critic probe I1_sealed_false_negative: block holds rare, summary says {common}. Under I1 the chain verified and the answer was empty. Under I1r the builder refuses the seal because row token rare is not in the summary, so the block is never committed with that summary; if a buggy builder sealed it anyway, the builder_version is in c_i and the test oracle catches it. Omitted block: ordinal gap against trusted n. Replaced head: root differs from trusted root. Prediction: every injected defect is rejected by path, count, digest or exclusion re-check, and no clean receipt fails.

title: I2r One-sync seal that fails closed on corruption and poisons on sync failure (repairs I2)
idea: Subtract the ordering sync, keep the failure contract. Frames plus one seal record (group length, SHA-256 over group bytes, previous seal digest) are written, then one sync. Reopen distinguishes three cases. (1) Incomplete tail: bytes end before a full seal, under a stated plausible-interruption rule (only the final group, only if no complete seal exists after it). Truncate it; it was never ACKed. (2) Full seal present with a hash mismatch: return a corruption error, preserve all bytes, and do not truncate; this applies to any previously committed group. (3) Match: accept. Any write or sync error poisons the handle; after an ambiguous failed sync, reopen refuses auto-resume without an independent recovery source, exactly as FOL2 does. No unconditional-recovery promise. Assumptions: single writer, sector-atomic writes at a stated size, a successful sync honoured, directory entry durable, SHA-256 collision resistance. The performance question is isolated: first group size 1 (one sync per event versus two), batching only afterwards.
kill_test: See prereg E2: logical sector model; enumerate sector subsets of the in-flight group, byte flips in committed groups, and injected write/sync errors; violations = outcomes outside the allowed set; kill if violations > 0. Non-vacuity: the original I2 truncate-on-mismatch rule must score violations > 0. A performance gate (group size 1, events/s and sync count vs two-sync) is a separate later registration.
thought_experiment: Critic probe I2_corrupt_acked_group: ACKed group with one flipped byte and a full seal. I2 truncated it (silent loss). I2r returns corruption and the file hash is unchanged. Interrupted tail with any subset of the last group's sectors persisted: truncate to the last matching seal, and no ACKed group is lost. Sync returns EIO: handle poisoned, no ACK, reopen flags that independent recovery is required. Prediction: every case lands in exactly one allowed outcome.

title: I3r Snapshot-bound residual answers with idempotent physical-coordinate merge (repairs I3)
idea: An answer is (R_c, q_r) where every row is keyed by physical coordinates (snapshot_head, block_ordinal, row_ordinal) and q_r binds snapshot head, the uncovered block ordinals and their content digests, predicate bytes, tokenizer version and order-semantics version. Merge is a set union keyed by coordinates, so retrying a residual cannot emit a row twice, and duplicate EventIds are preserved because identity is the coordinate, not the EventId. A residual presented against a different snapshot head, or a block whose digest changed (compaction, position reuse), is rejected, not merged. Permanently corrupt or unavailable blocks stay listed as unresolved; the system never claims eventual closure it cannot deliver.
kill_test: See prereg E3: seeded availability masks, retries, compactions with position reuse and corrupt blocks over fresh snapshots with duplicate EventIds; violations = closed answer != own-snapshot full scan + duplicate emissions + accepted cross-snapshot residual + false closure; kill if violations > 0. Non-vacuity: the original unbound I3 merge must fail the cross-snapshot case.
thought_experiment: Critic probe I3_cross_snapshot_residual: S = {0:A,1:B}, partial gives 0:A, compaction yields T = {0:B,1:C}, and the residual on T gives 1:C, so the merge is A,C (neither snapshot). Under I3r the residual carries head(S); T's head differs, so the residual is rejected, and the client must either re-run on T from scratch or obtain S's block 1. Retrying the residual on S twice yields 1:B once. Prediction: every closed answer equals the full scan of its own snapshot, and no cross-snapshot composition is accepted.

note: Counterexample from cross-family critic (CRITIQUE.md, critique_probes.py I1_sealed_false_negative, parent-reproduced exit 0): a freshly sealed false-negative summary verifies under the chain and the answer is empty; a chain head alone cannot authenticate per-block digests. Mutated into I7 (I1r).

Counterexample from critic (I2_corrupt_acked_group): the rule 'truncate the whole group on seal/hash mismatch' silently discards an ACKed group after post-sync corruption; it also left failed-sync ambiguity unaddressed. Mutated into I8 (I2r).
Counterexample from critic (I3_cross_snapshot_residual): an unbound residual merged across a compaction yields rows A,C equal to neither snapshot. Mutated into I9 (I3r).

Counterexample from critic (I4_two_stale_ledgers): two agreeing stale ledgers give an empty difference while the disk is empty; IBLT listing is probabilistic below capacity and loses multiplicity for identical retry tuples. The detector claim is withdrawn. Reconciling against an owner inventory rebuilt from verified raw bytes costs O(N) verification; only transmission can be O(d).
until: Fabric has (a) a sender ACK protocol whose ACK history persists independently after payloads are forgotten, (b) an owner inventory rebuilt from verified retained raw bytes or authenticated against an external witness (e.g. I7 roots), (c) stable (producer, sequence) identities with multiplicity or receiver dedup; then re-state it as an O(d)-transmission audit with explicit decode-failure and collision bounds.

note: Critic probe I5_single_thread_sync_shadow: on the current single-threaded FOL2 writer the summary is built after sync returns, so the free sync-shadow compute claim is withdrawn. Co-location removes staleness, not false negatives (semantic soundness needs I7's validated builder).
until: I7 survives E1 and a design either precomputes the summary from an immutable block before the frame sync or uses an explicit second worker whose CPU and critical path are measured; compare at equal block batching and sync schedule, not per-event FOL2 versus block commits.

note: Counterexample from critic (I6_cross_boundary_token): template time{v} with v=out reconstructs to 'timeout', which the S1 tokenizer matches, but neither piece contains it, so dictionary exclusion is a false negative despite a bit-identical round trip. The repair (index tokens of the reconstructed row) is known engineering in the CLP/LogGrep line [t:clp-efficient-and-scalable-search-on-compressed-text-logs, doi:10.1145/3552326.3567484], not a novelty claim.

Survives the critic after repair: closes T1 under explicit trust assumptions. Research promise: a Fabric-specific composition of known authenticated-data-structure mechanisms (vChain, hybrid authentication trees); not a new primitive.
Survives the critic after repair. Known engineering (OptFS, SQLite WAL checksummed commit frames); promoted for practical value against the append boundary (T2), not as a research novelty.

Survives the critic after repair. Research promise: executable, snapshot-bound exact residuals merged by physical coordinates; incomplete-answer semantics are known (Levy 1996, linked in CRITIQUE.md, not in the local cache).
